claims.claim: Microtubules, γ-TuRC components TBG-1/γ-tubulin and GIP-1/GCP3, and other MTOC and microtubule-associated proteins left the apical surface during mitosis.
claims.source: In addition to microtubules and the γ-TuRC components TBG-1/γ-tubulin and GIP-1/GCP3, all other MTOC and microtubule-associated proteins we examined also left the apical surface during mitosis (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 1E showing protein localization during mitosis.

claims.claim: Some MTOC proteins (γ-TuRC, ZYG-9/chTOG, AIR-1/Aurora A) localized to the active centrosomes during mitosis.
claims.source: Some MTOC proteins localized to the active centrosomes (γ-TuRC, ZYG-9/chTOG, AIR-1/Aurora A), while other proteins did not and likely became cytoplasmic (NOCA-1/Ninein, PTRN-1/CAMSAP, VAB-10B/Spectraplakin).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations of protein localization during mitosis.

claims.claim: Some MTOC proteins (NOCA-1/Ninein, PTRN-1/CAMSAP, VAB-10B/Spectraplakin) did not localize to active centrosomes and likely became cytoplasmic during mitosis.
claims.source: Some MTOC proteins localized to the active centrosomes (γ-TuRC, ZYG-9/chTOG, AIR-1/Aurora A), while other proteins did not and likely became cytoplasmic (NOCA-1/Ninein, PTRN-1/CAMSAP, VAB-10B/Spectraplakin).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations and inference about protein localization during mitosis.

claims.claim: The observed removal of apical MTOC proteins during mitosis, including the MTOC anchoring proteins VAB-10B and WDR-62, suggests the complete inactivation of the apical surface as an MTOC.
claims.source: The observed removal of apical MTOC proteins during mitosis, including the MTOC anchoring proteins VAB-10B and WDR-62 (Sanchez et al., 2020), suggests the complete inactivation of the apical surface as an MTOC.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed removal of MTOC proteins, supported by citation to Sanchez et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Junctional proteins retained some localization during mitosis, albeit reduced as compared with interphase neighboring cells.
claims.source: Junctional proteins retained some localization during mitosis, albeit reduced as compared with interphase neighboring cells (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 1F showing junctional protein localization during mitosis.

claims.claim: Localization of the septate-like junction-associated protein DLG-1/Discs large was most strongly reduced during mitosis.
claims.source: Localization of the septate-like junction-associated protein DLG-1/Discs large was most strongly reduced during mitosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, D), and the adherens junction protein HMR-1/E-cadherin was also reduced compared to the non-dividing 'non-star' intestinal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, E), appearing as thin fluorescent threads as new cell boundaries formed.
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, D.

claims.claim: The adherens junction protein HMR-1/E-cadherin was reduced during mitosis compared to the non-dividing 'non-star' intestinal cells, appearing as thin fluorescent threads as new cell boundaries formed.
claims.source: Localization of the septate-like junction-associated protein DLG-1/Discs large was most strongly reduced during mitosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, D), and the adherens junction protein HMR-1/E-cadherin was also reduced compared to the non-dividing 'non-star' intestinal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, E), appearing as thin fluorescent threads as new cell boundaries formed.
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, E.

claims.claim: ACT-5/actin and three members of the PAR complex PAR-3/Par3, PAR-6/Par6, and PKC-3/aPkc all remained apically localized during mitosis.
claims.source: The other apical proteins examined, ACT-5/actin and three members of the PAR complex PAR-3/Par3, PAR-6/Par6, and PKC-3/aPkc, all remained apically localized during mitosis (Figure 1G, H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, G).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 1G, H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, G.

claims.claim: PAR complex proteins actively mark the apical surface during mitotic remodeling to return apical MTOC function after division.
claims.source: Therefore, we hypothesized that PAR complex proteins actively mark the apical surface during mitotic remodeling to return apical MTOC function after division, thereby restoring a continuous apical MTOC.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that PAR complex proteins remain apical during mitosis.

claims.claim: In control embryos in which anterior star cells divided synchronously, a midline gap formed in the apical MTOC as centrosomes recruited additional TBG-1.
claims.source: In control embryos in which anterior star cells divided synchronously, a midline gap formed in the apical MTOC as centrosomes recruited additional TBG-1; MTOC proteins returned and filled the gap within 12 min as the centrosomes inactivated and shed TBG-1 (Figure 2E, F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 2E, F showing time-lapse imaging of MTOC during division.

claims.claim: In control embryos, MTOC proteins returned and filled the gap within 12 min as the centrosomes inactivated and shed TBG-1.
claims.source: In control embryos in which anterior star cells divided synchronously, a midline gap formed in the apical MTOC as centrosomes recruited additional TBG-1; MTOC proteins returned and filled the gap within 12 min as the centrosomes inactivated and shed TBG-1 (Figure 2E, F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 2E, F showing time-lapse imaging of MTOC during division.

claims.claim: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, midline MTOC gaps that formed during synchronous divisions persisted long after mitotic exit through the end of the time course, for a minimum of 24 min.
claims.source: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, however, midline MTOC gaps that formed during synchronous divisions persisted long after mitotic exit through the end of the time course, for a minimum of 24 min (Figure 2E, G).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 2E, G showing time-lapse imaging of MTOC in PAR-6gut(-) embryos.

claims.claim: The persistence of the midline gap in MTOC proteins in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) embryos is consistent with the hypothesis that PAR complex proteins promote the return of apical MTOC function after division.
claims.source: The persistence of the midline gap in MTOC proteins in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) embryos is consistent with our hypothesis that PAR complex proteins promote the return of apical MTOC function after division.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing persistent gaps in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) embryos.

claims.claim: In elongating control intestines, the apical MTOC remained continuous along the midline in both star cell daughters and in non-star cells.
claims.source: In elongating control intestines, the apical MTOC remained continuous along the midline in both star cell daughters and in non-star cells (Figure 3A, inset).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 3A showing MTOC continuity in control intestines.

claims.claim: In elongating PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines, midline gaps in MTOC proteins formed both in star cell daughters and in non-star cells that had not recently divided.
claims.source: By contrast, in elongating PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines, midline gaps in MTOC proteins formed both in star cell daughters and in non-star cells that had not recently divided (Figure 3B, C, insets); the midline gaps were clearly visualized by line scans (Figure 3B', C').
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 3B, C showing gaps in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines.

claims.claim: Only few PAR-6gut(-) embryos had small midline gaps in TBG-1 and PTRN-1 prior to the star cell divisions and elongation.
claims.source: Consistent with elongation causing gaps to form, we observed only few PAR-6gut(-) embryos with small midline gaps in TBG-1 and PTRN-1 prior to the star cell divisions and elongation (control: n = 1/17, PAR-6gut(-): n = 5/29).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data comparing gap frequency before and after elongation.

claims.claim: In control intestines, the apical MTOC stayed continuous as the average midline length increased approximately 80% in 50 min.
claims.source: In control intestines, the apical MTOC stayed continuous as the average midline length increased approximately 80% in 50 min (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 3D showing time-lapse imaging of control intestines.

claims.claim: In PAR-6gut(-) intestines, the apical MTOC formed gaps as the average apical surface elongated 70% in 50 min.
claims.source: In PAR-6gut(-) intestines, however, the apical MTOC formed gaps as the average apical surface elongated 70% in 50 min (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 3E showing time-lapse imaging of PAR-6gut(-) intestines.

claims.claim: 55.5% of PAR-6gut(-) and 44.4% of PKC-3gut(-) embryos had one or more gaps compared with 0% of control embryos.
claims.source: By these stringent criteria, 55.5% of PAR-6gut(-) and 44.4% of PKC-3gut(-) embryos had one or more gaps compared with 0% of control embryos (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 3F showing quantification of gaps.

claims.claim: 4.1% of PAR-6gut(-) and 3.7% of PKC-3gut(-) midline measurements were background level compared to 0% in control intestines.
claims.source: As a total proportion of the midline MTOC line scan signal, we found that 4.1% of PAR-6gut(-) and 3.7% of PKC-3gut(-) midline measurements were background level compared to 0% in control intestines (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 3G showing quantification of background-level measurements.

claims.claim: The number of background-level measurements increased over time in PAR-6gut(-) embryos but not in control embryos.
claims.source: The number of background-level measurements increased over time in PAR-6gut(-) embryos but not in control embryos (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 3H showing paired comparisons over time.

claims.claim: PAR-6 and PKC-3 are required for maintaining apical MTOC continuity between neighboring non-dividing cells during intestinal elongation.
claims.source: These results suggest that in addition to their roles in promoting continuity in dividing cells, PAR-6 and PKC-3 are also required for maintaining apical MTOC continuity between neighboring non-dividing cells during intestinal elongation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of gaps in non-dividing cells during elongation.

claims.claim: No physical separation between intestinal cells was detected in control, PAR-6gut(-), PKC-3gut(-), or CDC-42gut(-) embryos.
claims.source: We did not detect physical separation between intestinal cells in control, PAR-6gut(-), PKC-3gut(-), or CDC-42gut(-) embryos (Figure 4A–F); the membrane marker clearly spanned the gaps in TBG-1 (Figure 4B–D insets), and neighboring intestinal cells remained adjacent to each other.
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 4A–F showing membrane marker spanning gaps.

claims.claim: A higher frequency of gap formation was observed in the 8 star cells than in the 12 non-star cells in all three PAR complex depletion backgrounds.
claims.source: With intestinal cell membranes marked, we could also map which cells formed gaps within the intestine, and we observed a higher frequency of gap formation in the 8 star cells than in the 12 non-star cells in all three PAR complex depletion backgrounds (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 4F showing gap frequency in star vs. non-star cells.

claims.claim: Blocking star cell divisions with the cdc-25.2(0) mutation reduced the difference in gap frequency between star cells and non-star cells in PAR-6gut(-) embryos.
claims.source: While midline gaps were more frequent in PAR-6gut(-) star cells than non-star cells (star: 31% vs. non-star: 15%, Figure 4I), this difference in gap frequency was abrogated in PAR-6gut(-); cdc-25.2(0) double mutant embryos (star: 8% vs. non-star:19%, Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 4I showing gap frequency in PAR-6gut(-) vs. PAR-6gut(-); cdc-25.2(0) embryos.

claims.claim: PAR-6 is specifically required to protect MTOC continuity from disruption by cell division.
claims.source: This result suggests that PAR-6 is specifically required to protect MTOC continuity from disruption by cell division.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cdc-25.2(0) experiment showing reduced gap frequency when divisions are blocked.

claims.claim: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, apical YFP::ACT-5/actin formed gaps along the midline in both star cell daughters and in non-star cells.
claims.source: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, apical YFP::ACT-5/actin formed gaps along the midline in both star cell daughters and in non-star cells (10/19 and 9/19 gaps, respectively; Figure 5A, B), similar to MTOC protein gaps (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 5A, B showing ACT-5 gaps.

claims.claim: Midline gaps in PAR-3::tagRFP overlapped with gaps in PTRN-1::GFP in PAR-6gut(-) embryos.
claims.source: In addition, we found midline gaps in PAR-3::tagRFP, which normally localizes to the apical surface and junctions in the intestine (Achilleos et al., 2010; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), that overlapped with gaps in PTRN-1::GFP (Figure 5C, F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 5C, F showing overlapping gaps in PAR-3 and PTRN-1.

claims.claim: PAR-6 is essential for the general continuity of the apical domain during elongation.
claims.source: These results suggest that PAR-6 is essential not only for a continuous apical MTOC but also for the general continuity of the apical domain during elongation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of gaps in multiple apical markers.

claims.claim: 92% of TBG-1 gaps spanned the interface between adjacent cells in PAR-6gut(-) embryos.
claims.source: Our analysis of GFP::CAAX in PAR-6gut(-) embryos revealed that 92% of TBG-1 gaps spanned the interface between adjacent cells (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 4F showing gap location analysis.

claims.claim: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, HMR-1::GFP localized to the outer edge of the TBG-1 signal as expected for a junctional protein, but was generally absent from the TBG-1 midline gaps.
claims.source: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, HMR-1::GFP localized to the outer edge of the TBG-1 signal as expected for a junctional protein, but was generally absent from the TBG-1 midline gaps (Figure 5D, F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 5D, F showing HMR-1 localization relative to TBG-1 gaps.

claims.claim: DLG-1 was clearly absent from most TBG-1 gaps in PAR-6gut(-) embryos.
claims.source: We also examined DLG-1::mNG localization, which was severely perturbed along the entire midline in PAR-6gut(-) embryos as has previously been reported following PAR-6 depletion (Totong et al., 2007). We occasionally found large patches of DLG-1 that colocalized with TBG-1; however, DLG-1 was clearly absent from most TBG-1 gaps (Figure 5E, F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 5E, F showing DLG-1 localization relative to TBG-1 gaps, and citation to Totong et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Junctional complexes do not spread into and fill midline gaps in apical proteins following PAR-6 depletion.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that junctional complexes do not spread into and fill midline gaps in apical proteins following PAR-6 depletion.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that junctional proteins are absent from gaps.

claims.claim: In control intestines, LGL-1::GFP and LET-413::GFP were observed at lateral surfaces and strongly reduced at the midline where apical markers TBG-1::mCherry and PAR-3::tagRFP localized.
claims.source: In control intestines, LGL-1::GFP and LET-413::GFP were observed at lateral surfaces and strongly reduced at the midline where apical markers TBG-1::mCherry and PAR-3::tagRFP localized (Figure 5G–J).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 5G–J showing LGL-1 and LET-413 localization in control intestines.

claims.claim: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, LGL-1 and LET-413 signal intensities were significantly elevated in most gaps, and similar to intensities at lateral surfaces.
claims.source: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, LGL-1 and LET-413 signal intensities were significantly elevated in most gaps, and similar to intensities at lateral surfaces (Figure 5G–J).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 5G–J showing LGL-1 and LET-413 localization in PAR-6gut(-) embryos.

claims.claim: LGL-1 and LET-413 were also observed at midline 'non-gap' regions in PAR-6gut(-) embryos, where apical markers localized.
claims.source: LGL-1 and LET-413 were also observed at midline 'non-gap' regions, where apical markers localized (Figure 5G, I insets, orange arrowheads), suggesting a more general failure of LGL-1 and LET-413 exclusion from the apical surface rather than specific invasion of the basolateral domain into the midline gaps.
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 5G, I showing LGL-1 and LET-413 at non-gap midline regions.

claims.claim: The mislocalization of LGL-1 and LET-413 in PAR-6gut(-) embryos suggests a more general failure of LGL-1 and LET-413 exclusion from the apical surface rather than specific invasion of the basolateral domain into the midline gaps.
claims.source: LGL-1 and LET-413 were also observed at midline 'non-gap' regions, where apical markers localized (Figure 5G, I insets, orange arrowheads), suggesting a more general failure of LGL-1 and LET-413 exclusion from the apical surface rather than specific invasion of the basolateral domain into the midline gaps.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of LGL-1 and LET-413 at both gap and non-gap regions.

claims.claim: All PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae arrested as young L1 larvae.
claims.source: Indeed, all PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae arrested as young L1 larvae (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting that intestinal function was severely compromised.
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 6A showing larval arrest data.

claims.claim: Only 39% of CDC-42gut(-) larvae arrested as L1 larvae.
claims.source: Surprisingly, only 39% of CDC-42gut(-) larvae arrested as L1 larvae.
claims.evidence: Supported by larval arrest assay data.

claims.claim: In 98% of control larvae, blue food traveled through and filled the entire lumen without leaking into the body.
claims.source: In 98% of control larvae, blue food traveled through and filled the entire lumen without leaking into the body (Figure 6B, D).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 6B, D showing feeding assay results.

claims.claim: In 83% of PAR-6gut(-) larvae and 93% of PKC-3gut(-) larvae, blue food passed through the pharynx and pharyngeal valve but was trapped at the anterior end of the intestine, suggesting a luminal obstruction in the first intestinal ring (int1).
claims.source: However, in 83% of PAR-6gut(-) larvae and 93% of PKC-3gut(-) larvae, blue food passed through the pharynx and pharyngeal valve but was trapped at the anterior end of the intestine, suggesting a luminal obstruction in the first intestinal ring (int1), which comprises the four anterior star cell daughters (Figure 6B, E, F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 6B, E, F showing feeding assay results.

claims.claim: Blue food leaked into the body of 10% of PAR-6gut(-) and 2% of PKC-3gut(-) larvae.
claims.source: Blue food leaked into the body of a small percentage of larvae (10% of PAR-6gut(-), 2% of PKC-3gut(-)), suggesting that most of the PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae that ingested food retained their intestinal barrier function, at least between the pharyngeal valve and int1.
claims.evidence: Supported by feeding assay data.

claims.claim: Most PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae that ingested food retained their intestinal barrier function, at least between the pharyngeal valve and int1.
claims.source: Blue food leaked into the body of a small percentage of larvae (10% of PAR-6gut(-), 2% of PKC-3gut(-)), suggesting that most of the PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae that ingested food retained their intestinal barrier function, at least between the pharyngeal valve and int1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the low percentage of larvae with leaked food.

claims.claim: 42% of CDC-42gut(-) larvae had a normal intestine, 23% had an early int1 obstruction, and 20% had a more posterior obstruction.
claims.source: Consistent with their milder larval arrest phenotype, CDC-42gut(-) larvae also showed a lower penetrance of obstructed intestines; 42% had a normal intestine (Figure 6G), 23% had an early int1 obstruction (Figure 6G'), and 20% had a more posterior obstruction.
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 6G, G' showing feeding assay results for CDC-42gut(-) larvae.

claims.claim: When the star cell divisions in PAR-6gut(-) embryos were blocked with the cdc-25.2(0) mutation, a larger proportion of resulting larval intestines had a more posterior obstruction than PAR-6gut(-) larvae (25% vs. 5%).
claims.source: When the star cell divisions in PAR-6gut(-) embryos were blocked with the cdc-25.2(0) mutation, a larger proportion of resulting larval intestines had a more posterior obstruction than PAR-6gut(-) larvae (25% vs. 5%, Figure 6B, H).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 6B, H showing feeding assay results for PAR-6gut(-); cdc-25.2(0) larvae.

claims.claim: The defects imposed by the loss of PAR-6 in the dividing star cells could be rescued by blocking the anterior star cell divisions, allowing a continuous int1/int2 connection to form more frequently.
claims.source: These results indicate that the defects imposed by the loss of PAR-6 in the dividing star cells could be rescued by blocking the anterior star cell divisions, allowing a continuous int1/int2 connection to form more frequently.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cdc-25.2(0) rescue experiment.

claims.claim: PAR-6 is required during elongation itself and not just during earlier intestinal development.
claims.source: To determine if PAR-6 is required during elongation itself and not just during earlier intestinal development, we used a later promoter asp-1 to express intestinal ZIF-1 and degrade PAR-6 in 2-fold-stage embryos ('PAR-6late gut(-)'), after the star cells divided and before intestinal elongation completed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). We observed partially penetrant larval arrest (16%, Figure 6A) and obstructed lumen phenotypes (16%, Figure 6B, I, I'), consistent with a continued requirement for PAR-6 during embryonic intestinal elongation.
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 6A, B, I, I' and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showing late PAR-6 depletion results.

claims.claim: Wild-type PKC-3 was able to rescue the larval arrest and obstructed lumen defects and restore apical PAR-6 localization in PKC-3gut(-) embryos.
claims.source: We found that wild-type PKC-3 was able to rescue the larval arrest and obstructed lumen defects and restore apical PAR-6 localization in embryos (Figure 7A, E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, G).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 7A, E, F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, G showing rescue data.

claims.claim: The PAR-6-binding mutant PKC-3(ΔPB) showed almost no larval rescuing activity.
claims.source: As expected, the PAR-6-binding mutant showed almost no larval rescuing activity (Figure 7B, E, F), but surprisingly, embryos showed apical PAR-6 enrichment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, G).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 7B, E, F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, G showing rescue data.

claims.claim: Embryos expressing the PAR-6-binding mutant PKC-3(ΔPB) showed apical PAR-6 enrichment.
claims.source: As expected, the PAR-6-binding mutant showed almost no larval rescuing activity (Figure 7B, E, F), but surprisingly, embryos showed apical PAR-6 enrichment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, G).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, G showing PAR-6 localization data.

claims.claim: The PKC-3[G336N] kinase mutant partially rescued larval lethality and luminal obstruction and was strikingly similar to the CDC-42gut(-) phenotype.
claims.source: The PKC-3[G336N] kinase mutant partially rescued larval lethality and luminal obstruction and was strikingly similar to the CDC-42gut(-) phenotype (Figure 7C, C', E, F); by contrast, the PKC-3[K282A] kinase mutant showed almost no larval rescuing activity (Figure 7D–F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 7C, C', E, F showing rescue data.

claims.claim: The PKC-3[K282A] kinase mutant showed almost no larval rescuing activity.
claims.source: The PKC-3[G336N] kinase mutant partially rescued larval lethality and luminal obstruction and was strikingly similar to the CDC-42gut(-) phenotype (Figure 7C, C', E, F); by contrast, the PKC-3[K282A] kinase mutant showed almost no larval rescuing activity (Figure 7D–F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 7D–F showing rescue data.

claims.claim: Both PKC-3 kinase mutants restored apical PAR-6 enrichment in embryos.
claims.source: The two kinase mutants had differing levels of rescuing activity, though both restored apical PAR-6 enrichment in embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–G).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–G showing PAR-6 localization data.

claims.claim: Apical PAR-6 localization is not sufficient to restore apical continuity and viability.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that apical PAR-6 localization is not sufficient to restore apical continuity and viability, and that PKC-3 kinase activity and PAR-6-binding are both critical for normal PKC-3 function and for apical continuity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that PAR-6 localization alone is not sufficient.

claims.claim: PKC-3 kinase activity and PAR-6-binding are both critical for normal PKC-3 function and for apical continuity.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that apical PAR-6 localization is not sufficient to restore apical continuity and viability, and that PKC-3 kinase activity and PAR-6-binding are both critical for normal PKC-3 function and for apical continuity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments.

claims.claim: The lumens of PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines frequently appeared to be pinched shut in multiple places, often with edematous swellings.
claims.source: Unlike the continuous open lumen of control intestines (Figure 8A), the lumens of PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines frequently appeared to be pinched shut in multiple places, often with edematous swellings (Figure 8B, C, E), and PAR-6late gut(-) lumens also appeared pinched shut in one or two places in some larvae (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), consistent with a continued requirement for PAR-6 during elongation.
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 8B, C, E showing larval intestinal morphology.

claims.claim: CDC-42gut(-) larvae generally had one or two points of luminal constriction, but the overall intestinal morphology was not as severely defective as in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae.
claims.source: CDC-42gut(-) larvae generally had one or two points of luminal constriction (Figure 8D), but the overall intestinal morphology was not as severely defective as in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae.
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 8D showing CDC-42gut(-) larval intestinal morphology.

claims.claim: All PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines had one or more int interface with a constricted lumen.
claims.source: While control intestines clearly had an open lumen between int rings, PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines all had one or more int interface with a constricted lumen, and CDC-42gut(-) larvae again showed a milder phenotype (Figure 8F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 8F showing quantification of luminal constrictions.

claims.claim: Most PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae and 50% of CDC-42gut(-) larvae had their lumens pinched shut within int1.
claims.source: Further, most PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae and 50% of CDC-42gut(-) larvae had their lumens pinched shut within int1 (Figure 8G), consistent with the int1 obstruction and accumulation of blue-dyed food in the feeding assay and with the anterior star cell midline gaps caused by cell division.
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 8G showing quantification of int1 constrictions.

claims.claim: PAR-6 and PKC-3 are essential during embryonic development to build an intestine with a continuous open lumen.
claims.source: Thus, PAR-6 and PKC-3 are essential during embryonic development to build an intestine with a continuous open lumen.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the larval intestinal morphology data.

claims.claim: PAR-3 localized to hollow sphere-like structures that were often separated by gaps in localization in PAR-6gut(-) larvae, unlike the continuous luminal PAR-3 in control L1 larval intestines.
claims.source: Unlike the continuous luminal PAR-3 in control L1 larval intestines, PAR-3 localized to hollow sphere-like structures that were often separated by gaps in localization in PAR-6gut(-) larvae (Figure 9A–C), consistent with a polarized but discontinuous luminal surface.
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 9A–C showing PAR-3 localization in larvae.

claims.claim: All PAR-6gut(-) larvae and some PAR-6late gut(-) larvae showed gaps in luminal ACT-5.
claims.source: ACT-5 is strongly expressed in larval intestines and localizes to the apical brush border (MacQueen et al., 2005), and unlike the continuous luminal ACT-5 in control larvae, all PAR-6gut(-) larvae and some PAR-6late gut(-) larvae showed gaps in luminal ACT-5 (Figure 9D–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 9D–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D showing ACT-5 localization in larvae, and citation to MacQueen et al., 2005.

claims.claim: All PAR-6gut(-) larvae had DLG-1 bands that were clearly discontinuous between adjacent int rings in multiple places.
claims.source: We also found DLG-1 localization to be defective. While control intestines contained a continuous ladder-like belt arrangement of DLG-1, all PAR-6gut(-) larvae had DLG-1 bands that were clearly discontinuous between adjacent int rings in multiple places (Figure 9G–I).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 9G–I showing DLG-1 localization in larvae.

claims.claim: In control larvae, LGL-1 was clearly excluded from apical surfaces along the midline.

results.result: During mitosis in C. elegans intestinal star cells, apical PAR complex proteins (PAR-6, PKC-3, PAR-3) and actin remain apically localized, while apical microtubules and MTOC proteins (including γ-TuRC components, ZYG-9, AIR-1, NOCA-1, PTRN-1, VAB-10B) are transiently removed from the apical surface. Some MTOC proteins relocalize to active centrosomes while others become cytoplasmic. This creates a visible 'midline gap' in MTOC proteins during synchronous star cell divisions that is refilled upon mitotic exit.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C39-C45 are well-supported by live imaging data presented in Figures 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements showing protein localization during mitosis. The differential behavior of PAR complex proteins versus MTOC proteins during mitosis is clearly documented with multiple protein markers and quantification (Figure 1E-H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The transient nature of MTOC removal and gap formation is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging.

results.result: Junctional proteins (HMR-1/E-cadherin and DLG-1/Discs large) retain some localization during mitosis but are reduced compared to interphase neighboring cells, with DLG-1 showing the strongest reduction and HMR-1 appearing as thin fluorescent threads at new cell boundaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by imaging data in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, D-E showing junctional protein localization during mitosis with quantification demonstrating significant reduction compared to non-dividing cells. The differential reduction of DLG-1 versus HMR-1 is documented.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that PAR complex proteins (PAR-3, PAR-6, PKC-3) actively mark the apical surface during mitotic remodeling to facilitate the return of apical MTOC function after division, based on their observation that these proteins remain apically localized during mitosis while MTOC proteins are removed.
results.evaluation: Claim C49 is well-supported by imaging data (Figure 1G-H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, G), but C50 is a hypothesis/speculation rather than a demonstrated result. While the observation that PAR proteins remain apical during mitosis is solid, the mechanistic claim that they 'actively mark' the surface to facilitate MTOC return requires additional functional evidence beyond localization data.

results.result: Intestine-specific depletion of PAR-6, PKC-3, or CDC-42 causes persistent gaps in the apical MTOC after cell division. In control embryos, MTOC gaps formed during synchronous star cell divisions are refilled within 12 minutes, but in PAR-6gut(-) embryos, these gaps persist for at least 24 minutes after mitotic exit.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 and C51-C54 are strongly supported by experimental data from tissue-specific protein depletion experiments shown in Figure 2. Time-lapse imaging (Figure 2E-G) clearly demonstrates the differential kinetics of gap closure between control and PAR-6gut(-) embryos with quantification. The use of the ZIF-1/ZF degradation system is well-validated and protein depletion is confirmed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

results.result: PAR-6 and PKC-3 are required for maintaining apical MTOC continuity during intestinal elongation in both dividing star cells and non-dividing non-star cells. In PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) embryos, midline gaps in MTOC proteins form and increase over time during elongation, with 55.5% of PAR-6gut(-) and 44.4% of PKC-3gut(-) embryos showing one or more gaps compared to 0% of controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C55-C63 are well-supported by extensive imaging and quantification data in Figure 3. Time-lapse imaging demonstrates gap formation during elongation (Figure 3D-E), and stringent quantitative criteria are used to define gaps (Figure 3F-H). The observation that gaps form in both star and non-star cells, and increase over time specifically in PAR-6gut(-) embryos, is clearly documented. The methodology for gap quantification is described in detail in Materials and Methods.

results.result: Midline gaps in MTOC proteins occur at cell-cell interfaces without physical cell separation. Star cells show higher gap frequency than non-star cells in all PAR complex depletion backgrounds. Blocking star cell divisions with cdc-25.2(0) mutation reduces the difference in gap frequency between star and non-star cells in PAR-6gut(-) embryos, suggesting PAR-6 is specifically required to protect MTOC continuity from disruption by cell division.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 and C115 are supported by data in Figure 4 using membrane markers to map gap locations and the cdc-25.2(0) genetic experiment. The membrane marker GFP::CAAX clearly spans gaps (Figure 4B-D), demonstrating no physical separation. Gap frequency analysis (Figure 4F, I) shows higher frequency in star cells, and the cdc-25.2(0) rescue experiment (Figure 4G-I) provides genetic evidence for the role of division in gap formation. However, the causal interpretation in C67 and C115 is somewhat inferential.

results.result: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, gaps form not only in MTOC proteins but also in other apical markers including ACT-5/actin and PAR-3, suggesting PAR-6 is essential for general continuity of the apical domain during elongation.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are supported by imaging data in Figure 5A-C showing gaps in multiple apical markers (ACT-5, PAR-3) that overlap with MTOC protein gaps. The inference in C70 that PAR-6 is essential for 'general' apical continuity is reasonable given the multiple markers affected, though the term 'general' could be more precisely defined.

results.result: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, 92% of MTOC gaps span cell-cell interfaces. Junctional proteins (HMR-1, DLG-1) are generally absent from these gaps, indicating that junctional complexes do not spread into and fill midline gaps in apical proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 are supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 4F and Figure 5D-F. The localization of junctional markers relative to MTOC gaps is clearly shown, with HMR-1 localizing to the outer edge of TBG-1 signal and DLG-1 being absent from most gaps. The inference in C74 is reasonable based on the localization data.

results.result: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, basolateral markers LGL-1 and LET-413 show significantly elevated signal intensity in midline gaps (similar to lateral surface levels) and are also observed at midline non-gap regions where apical markers localize, suggesting a general failure of basolateral protein exclusion from the apical surface rather than specific invasion into gaps.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 are supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 5G-J. The signal intensity measurements clearly show elevated LGL-1 and LET-413 in gaps compared to control midlines, and the presence of these proteins at non-gap midline regions is documented. The interpretation in C78 is a reasonable inference from the data, though alternative explanations are not fully excluded.

results.result: PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae arrest as L1 larvae with intestinal luminal obstructions that block food passage. In 83% of PAR-6gut(-) and 93% of PKC-3gut(-) larvae, food is trapped at the anterior intestine (int1), while 98% of control larvae have normal food passage. CDC-42gut(-) larvae show a milder phenotype with only 39% arresting at L1. Most larvae retain barrier function with minimal leakage.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C79-C85 are well-supported by larval arrest assays (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1) and feeding assays (Figure 6B-G', Figure 6—source data 2). The phenotypic penetrance is clearly quantified across multiple trials. The inference in C84 about retained barrier function is reasonable given the low leakage frequency, though this is somewhat indirect evidence.

results.result: Blocking star cell divisions with cdc-25.2(0) in PAR-6gut(-) embryos shifts the luminal obstruction phenotype from predominantly int1 (83%) to more posterior locations (25% vs 5% in PAR-6gut(-) alone), suggesting that defects from loss of PAR-6 in dividing star cells can be partially rescued by preventing division.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by feeding assay data in Figure 6B, H showing the shift in obstruction location when divisions are blocked. The interpretation in C87 is a reasonable inference from the genetic rescue experiment, though the mechanism of rescue is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: PAR-6 is required during elongation itself and not just during earlier intestinal development, as demonstrated by later-stage depletion (PAR-6late gut(-)) using asp-1 promoter resulting in partially penetrant larval arrest (16%) and obstructed lumen phenotypes (16%).
results.evaluation: Claim C88 is supported by the late depletion experiment shown in Figure 6A, B, I, I' and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A. The timing of degradation is documented, and the partially penetrant phenotype is consistent with later-stage requirement. However, the penetrance is much lower than early depletion, which could reflect incomplete degradation or a lesser requirement at later stages.

results.result: PKC-3 rescue experiments demonstrate that wild-type PKC-3 rescues larval arrest and luminal defects, while PAR-6-binding mutant (ΔPB) and kinase-dead mutant (K282A) show minimal rescue despite restoring apical PAR-6 localization. The G336N kinase mutant shows partial rescue similar to CDC-42gut(-) phenotype. These results demonstrate that apical PAR-6 localization is insufficient for function and that both PKC-3 kinase activity and PAR-6 binding are critical.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C96 are supported by comprehensive rescue experiments in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. Multiple independent transgenic lines were tested for each construct, and both larval arrest and feeding assays were performed. The key finding that PAR-6 localization is restored by mutant PKC-3 but function is not rescued (C95-C96) is well-demonstrated. However, the interpretation of G336N as specifically affecting kinase activity (C92, C155) versus being hypomorphic (C156) remains uncertain.

results.result: PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larval intestines have lumens that are pinched shut in multiple places with edematous swellings. All PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines have one or more int interface with constricted lumen, and most have lumens pinched shut within int1. CDC-42gut(-) larvae show milder defects. PAR-6 and PKC-3 are essential for building an intestine with a continuous open lumen.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C101 are supported by detailed morphological analysis in Figure 8 using membrane markers and DIC imaging. The quantification of luminal constrictions at int interfaces (Figure 8F-G) is systematic and clearly shows the severity and location of defects. The conclusion in C101 is well-supported by the combined data from embryonic gaps and larval luminal defects.

results.result: In PAR-6gut(-) L1 larvae, apical markers (PAR-3, ACT-5) show discontinuous localization with gaps, junctional marker DLG-1 shows discontinuous bands between int rings, and basolateral marker LGL-1 shows partial midline localization. These results suggest that early embryonic gaps in apical and junctional proteins persist through morphogenesis, leading to discontinuous apical surfaces and junctions in larvae.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C107 are supported by larval imaging data in Figure 9 showing persistent defects in multiple markers. The correlation between embryonic gaps and larval defects (C107, C133) is demonstrated through the progression of phenotypes, though direct lineage tracing of specific gaps from embryo to larva is not performed. The inference is reasonable but somewhat indirect.

results.result: Tissue-specific protein degradation was critical for this study, allowing bypass of embryonic lethality from ubiquitous PAR-6, PKC-3, or CDC-42 depletion. This approach revealed that PAR-6 and PKC-3 are required embryonically to build a functional intestine but appear dispensable once built, suggesting embryonic and larval intestines elongate via different mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C112 are supported by the successful application of tissue-specific degradation and comparison with prior work showing embryonic lethality from ubiquitous depletion (C109, citations provided). The inference about differential mechanisms (C112) is reasonable based on the late depletion experiments showing reduced penetrance, though direct mechanistic evidence is not provided. The caveat that tissue-specific degradation is not equivalent to null (C146) is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Dividing star cells are particularly sensitive to PAR-6, PKC-3, and CDC-42 depletion. Although star cells contribute only three of nine int rings, over half of midline gaps in 1.5-fold embryos affect star cell daughters. Cell division appears to cause this high gap frequency as inhibiting divisions ameliorates gaps.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 are supported by gap frequency analysis (Figure 4F) and the cdc-25.2(0) genetic experiment (Figure 4I). The disproportionate effect on star cells is clearly documented. However, the causal statement in C115 is somewhat inferential - while blocking divisions reduces gaps, this could reflect either a direct effect of division or an indirect effect of having fewer cells to maintain continuity.

results.result: The primary defect in PAR-6-, PKC-3-, and CDC-42-depleted intestines is failure to maintain coordination of apicobasal polarity between cells. Apical and junctional gaps correlate with luminal gaps that block food passage. Despite severe luminal defects, barrier function is largely intact with rare leakage. DLG-1 appears to recover junction-like localization in larvae, suggesting a secondary mechanism may drive septate-like junction formation independent of PAR-6 and PKC-3. These proteins maintain apical and junctional continuity rather than being required for lumen formation per se.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C138 and C148 represent the authors' synthesis of results. The correlation between gaps and luminal defects (C133) is well-documented. The retention of barrier function (C134) is supported by low leakage frequency, though this is somewhat unexpected given junction defects (C135). The recovery of DLG-1 in larvae (C136-C137) is observed, and the speculation about secondary mechanisms (C138) is reasonable but not directly tested. The overall conclusion (C148) is well-supported by the totality of data, though the caveat about tissue-specific degradation not being equivalent to null (C146-C147) is important.

results.result: CDC-42 shows tissue-specific requirements distinct from other tissues. While CDC-42 is required for PAR complex localization in many tissues, it is not required for apical polarity establishment in the intestine. Intestine-specific CDC-42 depletion revealed a role in promoting apical continuity after polarity establishment. CDC-42gut(-), PAR-6gut(-), and PKC-3gut(-) embryos show similar embryonic gaps, but only PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae show increased gaps, suggesting CDC-42 is required early while PAR-6 and PKC-3 are required throughout elongation.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C153 are supported by comparison of phenotypes across genotypes (Figures 3-9) and prior work (citations provided). The differential severity in larvae (C152) is clearly documented. The interpretation about temporal requirements (C153) is a reasonable inference from the data, though direct temporal analysis of CDC-42 requirement is not performed. The tissue-specific difference in CDC-42 requirement (C150-C151) is well-established by prior work and confirmed here.

results.result: The differential rescue by PKC-3 kinase mutants suggests CDC-42 may activate PKC-3 kinase activity, with PAR-6 and PKC-3 also providing kinase-independent activity. The G336N mutant partially rescues with phenotype similar to CDC-42gut(-), while K282A completely abolishes rescue. However, G336N could be acting as a hypomorphic mutation rather than specifically affecting kinase activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C156 represent speculation about mechanisms based on the rescue data (Figure 7). While the differential rescue by G336N versus K282A is clearly demonstrated (C155), the mechanistic interpretations (C154, C156) are speculative. The similarity between G336N rescue and CDC-42gut(-) phenotype is noted but does not definitively establish that CDC-42 activates kinase activity. The alternative explanation that G336N is hypomorphic (C156) is equally plausible. Additional biochemical experiments would be needed to distinguish these possibilities.

results.result: The authors propose several speculative mechanisms for why dividing cells are sensitive to PAR complex depletion: (1) loss of apical microtubules during mitosis weakens epithelial integrity, making cells more dependent on PAR complex; (2) apical microtubules and PAR-6 may redundantly maintain the apical domain; (3) division requires new junction formation that relies on PAR complex proteins; (4) synchronous division of neighboring cells removes positional information from junctions. Supporting these ideas, HMR-1 and DLG-1 levels are drastically reduced during synchronous divisions, and PAR-6gut(-) gaps form during synchronous but not asynchronous divisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C126 mix established facts (C116, C118, C121, C123-C124) with speculation (C117, C119, C120, C122, C125-C126). The observations about junctional protein reduction during synchronous divisions (C123) and gap formation only during synchronous divisions in PAR-6gut(-) (C124) are well-supported by data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). However, the mechanistic interpretations (C117, C119, C122, C125-C126) are speculative and not directly tested. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: The midline gap phenotype becomes more severe during the threefold increase in intestine length to L1 stage. Later PAR-6 depletion also causes discontinuous lumens, confirming continued requirement during elongation. Most gaps occur at anterior-posterior cell interfaces without physical separation. Basolateral protein localization to gaps is not specific, suggesting compromised apical/junctional expansion allows basolateral protein diffusion rather than basolateral invasion creating gaps.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C131 are supported by comparison of embryonic and larval phenotypes (Figures 3, 8-9) and late depletion experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The observation about gap locations (C129) is documented in Figure 4F. The interpretation about basolateral protein localization (C130-C131) is reasonable based on the observation that LGL-1 and LET-413 are present at both gap and non-gap midline regions (Figure 5G-J), though the mechanistic speculation in C131 is not directly tested.

results.result: The authors speculate about mechanisms of lumen formation and barrier function in PAR-6gut(-) larvae. They propose the Crumbs complex as a candidate parallel pathway for junction formation. They note that luminal regions with apical proteins form despite PAR-6 loss, suggesting lumenogenesis machinery is intact. They favor a model where edematous swellings result from normal lumenogenesis with no exit route for luminal fluid, rather than dysregulated luminal expansion.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C145 are largely speculative. The Crumbs complex as a candidate pathway (C139-C141) is reasonable speculation based on prior work but not tested here. The observation that luminal regions with apical proteins form (C142) is supported by imaging data (Figure 9), and the inference about intact lumenogenesis is reasonable. However, the model for edematous swellings (C143-C145) is speculative and not directly tested. The observation that luminal expansion is usually associated with increased apical proteins (C144) makes the edema somewhat paradoxical, and the proposed model (C145) is one possible explanation but not demonstrated.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on epithelial polarity, the PAR complex, C. elegans intestinal development, and prior work on PAR complex function in the intestine. This includes established knowledge about epithelial cell polarity, junctions, microtubule organization, PAR complex composition and function, and C. elegans intestinal anatomy and development.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C38 represent background knowledge and prior work, all supported by appropriate citations. These provide essential context for the study but are not novel results. The anatomical descriptions of C. elegans intestine (C31-C38) are well-established and supported by the authors' own imaging (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements).

results.result: The authors conclude that apicobasal polarity regulators are highly conserved yet differentially required across organisms and tissues, with the same gene having different functions in different contexts. They emphasize the importance of detailed studies of diverse epithelia for understanding polarity protein function in development and disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C159 represent the authors' perspective on the broader significance of their work. C157-C158 are supported by citations to prior work showing differential requirements and context-dependent functions. C159 is a statement about the value of future research that is reasonable given the findings of this study demonstrating tissue-specific requirements.
